Rock salt: Reference: drift emplacement of POLLUX casks; alternatives: CASTOR casks in short horizontal boreholes, canisters in vertical boreholes up to 300 m deep
Claystone: Horizontal drift emplacement of supercontainers, or vertical borehole emplacement of BSK-R canisters
Crystalline rock: Vertical borehole emplacement of copper canisters (BSK-Cu); KBS-3: vertical short boreholes approx. 8 m deep with bentonite buffer

Rock salt: Geological barrier (containment-providing rock zone); crushed salt backfill and seals close the excavations
Claystone: Geological barrier (low permeability, diffusion-dominated transport, sorption); supported by containers and bentonite buffer
Crystalline rock: Engineered barriers: canister has the primary safety function, plus bentonite buffer; host rock contributes little to containment
Source: Salt: GRS-471 Anh. 5, p. 15; clay: GRS-471 sect. 2.1.2.1, pp. 35–36; crystalline: GRS-471 sect. 2.1.2.2, p. 37

Rock salt: High rock temperatures (up to 200 °C) near emplacement areas, so re-excavated drifts need cooling by ventilation; high solubility of salt
Claystone: Low rock strength, so heavy support needed (rock bolts, shotcrete, steel arches); ventilation must limit moisture entering the clay; working air max. 30 °C effective temperature
Crystalline rock: Stability controlled by joints; support only in heavily fractured sections; water inflow through fractured zones; working air max. 30 °C effective temperature
Source: Salt: GRS-471 Anh. 5, pp. 21–22 and BGR 2007, K-MAT 7, Tab. 1; clay: GRS-471 Tab. 2.1, pp. 14 and 19, sect. 2.1.2.1; crystalline: GRS-471 Tab. 2.1, p. 19, sect. 2.1.2.2 and BGR 2007, Tab. 1

Claystone: German generic concept, reference regions in northern and southern Germany, 300–800 m; international: Cigéo at Bure, France (525 m)
